questions.q: Name the four official racial categories created by the Population Registration Act of 1950 under apartheid.
questions.a: The four categories were White, Black (referred to as "Bantu" or "Native" in legislation), Coloured (mixed ancestry), and Indian/Asian. A wrong answer (e.g., listing "African" and "Black" separately, or adding "Asian" as a fifth category) reveals the student is confusing popular terminology with the legal definitions used by the apartheid state — a critical error because exam questions often quote the Act's exact language.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the Group Areas Act (1950) was more destructive than simple social segregation.
questions.a: The Group Areas Act legally forced physical relocation: entire communities were uprooted from homes and land they owned, bulldozed (e.g., District Six, Sophiatown), and dumped in distant, under-resourced townships — destroying generational wealth, social networks, and access to jobs. A wrong answer that describes it as "people choosing to live apart" or "separate neighbourhoods" misses the state violence, economic dispossession, and the fact that Black people could not own land in "White" areas — a distinction that carries 2-3 marks in board answers.

questions.q: A Black South African worker in 1970s Johannesburg holds a "pass book" under the Native Laws Amendment Act. He is stopped by police 5 km from his township job. What specific crime has he committed if his pass does not have a valid employer signature for that district?
questions.a: He has committed the crime of being in a "White" area without authorization — specifically, failing to produce a valid Section 10(1)(b) endorsement proving he has permission to seek or hold work there. The pass book (dompas) controlled movement, not just identity. A wrong answer like "he forgot his ID" shows the student doesn't grasp that the pass system criminalized Black presence in cities unless serving White economic interests — a concept essential for analyzing Mandela's description of "the grim reality of the pass laws."

questions.q: Compare the impact of the Bantu Education Act (1953) on Black students with the impact of the Separate Amenities Act (1953) on daily life. Which law had a longer-term generational consequence? Justify.
questions.a: Bantu Education had deeper generational impact: it deliberately designed an inferior curriculum ("education for servitude") limiting Black children to manual labour skills, creating a structural skills gap that persists today. Separate Amenities Act segregated buses, benches, toilets — humiliating and inconvenient, but reversible by policy change. A wrong answer that picks Separate Amenities because "it affected everyone daily" confuses visibility with structural depth. Board examiners reward answers that link Bantu Education to the economic disempowerment Mandela fought against.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "Apartheid was essentially the same as racial segregation in the southern USA (Jim Crow laws)." Defend or refute using two specific differences in legal structure or state enforcement.
questions.a: Refute. Difference 1: Apartheid was a comprehensive, centrally legislated system with a racial classification bureaucracy (Population Registration Act) that assigned race at birth and controlled every aspect of life — Jim Crow was a patchwork of state/local statutes without a federal racial registry. Difference 2: Apartheid created "homelands" (Bantustans) to strip Black citizens of South African citizenship, making them foreigners in their own country — Jim Crow never revoked US citizenship. A wrong answer that says "both were bad" or "both separated races" fails to analyze the unique totalitarian architecture of apartheid, a distinction CBSE competency questions often test.

questions.q: Write a 50-word diary entry from the perspective of a 16-year-old Coloured student in Cape Town, 1976, describing how the Population Registration Act and Group Areas Act have shaped your family's life. Use the terms "reclassified" and "forced removal" correctly.
questions.a: Sample: "Yesterday the Population Registration Board reclassified my older brother from 'Coloured' to 'White' — he can now vote, but cannot live with us. Last year the Group Areas Act forced our removal from District Six to the Cape Flats; my father's commute doubled, my mother lost her clinic. We are strangers in our own city." A poor answer uses the terms as decoration without showing the legal machinery tearing families apart — revealing the student memorized vocabulary but not the human mechanism of apartheid.
